I manually select my context (like a caveman) and clear it often... it looks like something I've been doing all along - though I informally referred to it as the 'Table of Contents' approach.

So far I am in the skeptic camp on this. I don't see it adding a lot of value to my current claude code workflow which already includes specialized agents and a custom mcp... I also think 'skills' is a bad name.
I've switched a few MCP servers to just scripts because they were taking like 20% of the context just by being there. Now, I can ask the model to use X script, which it reads and uses only if needed.
if you've ever worked with Excel + Python... There are many edge cases when writing / reading Excel files with Python and this [Anthropic xlsx skill] nails many of them.
Experimenting with skills over the last few months has completely changed the way I think about using LLMs... when it doesn't work, it is as much a problem with our tools as it is with the LLM.
Does anyone find that agents just don't use them without being asked?
I often find they aren't triggered when I would expect using a keyword and explicitly trigger them.
'skills' are just .md files that the lossy compressing statistical output machine may or may not find and that may or may not be retained in the tiny context window

I have an incredibly hard time getting them to use Skills at all, even when asked. I saw someone's analysis... their agents were more accurate when just dumping the skill context directly into AGENTS.md
If I put the skill's instructions in the general AGENTS.md, it works just fine.
This has been a problem for us too. Sometimes they reach for skills, sometimes they don't and just try to do the thing on their own. It's annoying.

Same, I have a bunch of skills defined with proper YAML headers and semantic triggers installed... Even with that, I have to be very specific in triggering a skill and it's hit or miss if it picks up on the skill.

I use codex and it seems to mostly stick to instructions I give. I use an AGENTS.md that explicitly points to the repository's skill directory... Probably the more skills you have, the more confused it might get.

I started playing with skills yesterday. I'm not sure if it's just easier for the LLM to call APIs inside the skill... I have a feeling that otherwise it becomes too messy for agents to reliably handle a lot of complex stuff.
